text: Continued misuse of multiple testing correction methods in population genetics‐A wake‐up call?

Population geneticists often use multiple independent hypothesis tests of Hardy– Weinberg Equilibrium (HWE), Linkage Disequilibrium (LD), and population differenti- ation, to make broad inferences about their systems of choice. However, correcting for Family‐Wise Error Rates (FWER) that are inflated due to multiple comparisons, is sparingly reported in our current literature. In this issue of Molecular Ecology Resources, perform a meta‐analysis of 215 population genetics studies published between 2011 and 2013 to show (i) scarce use of FWER corrections across all three classes of tests, and (ii) when used, inconsistent application of correction methods with a clear bias towards less‐conservative corrections for tests of population differ- entiation, than for tests of HWE, and LD. Here we replicate this meta‐analysis using 205 population genetics studies published between 2013 and 2018, to show the same continued disuse, and inconsistencies. We hope that both studies serve as a wake‐up call to population geneticists, reviewers, and editors to be rigorous about Bonferroni, FWER, multiple comparisons, population genetics—empirical, type I error A lot has been said about the interpretation and subsequent misin- terpretation of the “innocent” (Kuffner & Walker, 2018), yet blasé p‐ value. Simplistically, a p‐value is a measure of concordance with a null hypothesis, but often misinterpreted as a metric of “truth” of the null hypothesis itself (Altman & Krzywinski, 2017). As population geneticists, we often see these p‐values coupled with yet another controversial word, “significance” (or lack thereof). It should come as no surprise that several “significant” discoveries in our field are often based on unjustified over‐interpretation of p‐values. Commonly, the critical value threshold is arbitrarily set to 0.05 (the history behind this dates back to Fisher—Fisher, 2006). Interpreted at its surface, for a statistical test like a test of Hardy Weinberg Equilibrium (HWE), Linkage Disequilibrium (LD), or population differentiation— for example, Fst, Gst, if the probability of observing a more extreme test statistic than the observed data distribution if the null hypothe- sis is true is less than the critical value, then the implication is that one would incorrectly infer that the null hypothesis is false, when it is actually true, 5% of the times, resulting in a false positive (type 1 error). When performing statistical inference across multiple tests, the rate of incorrectly rejecting the null hypothesis across all tests is estimated by the FWER, 1‐(1‐α)k, where α is the set threshold for the p‐value (significance level). Correspondingly, the true positive rate across the family of tests declines. This problem is often exacer- bated in population genetics tests when: tests of HWE are con- ducted across multiple genomic loci and across multiple sampled locales; tests of LD are conducted across multiple pairs of genomic Received: 14 September 2018 | Revised: 2 November 2018 | Accepted: 12 November 2018 Mol Ecol Resour. 2019;19:23–26. wileyonlinelibrary.com/journal/men © 2019 John Wiley & Sons Ltd | 23 loci; and tests of genetic differentiation are conducted across and between multiple genomic loci and different subpopulations, respec- tively. Numerous corrections have been proposed in the literature, including the most commonly applied FWER Bonferroni correction (most stringent—but with higher probability of false negatives, due to erroneously adjudging a truly significant result to be false, which is due to a more conservative p‐value cut‐off), sequential Bonferroni corrections (Holm, 1979) and the False Discovery Rate (FDR) correc- tion methods of Benjamini and Hochberg (1995—B‐H method) and Benjamini and Yekutieli (2001—B‐Y method). The FDR correction methods are less “stringent” than FWER corrections and as a result, have greater power when performing multiple independent or dependent comparisons. Nevertheless, both corrective methods are easy to perform, and provide greater power when performing multi- ple comparisons (Narum, 2006, but also refer to an erratum in White, Ende, & Nichols, 2018 regarding computing the FDR critical values in the B‐Y method). However, in our inherent quest for “sig- nificant” discovery, we may unconsciously or consciously avoid the application of corrective methods, or when applied, use them incon- sistently. In this issue of MER, Hauser et al. discuss this very issue through a meta‐analysis of 215 population genetics studies that have appeared in peer‐reviewed literature between 2011 and 2013. The results of this study explain that 27% of all studies did not report tests of HWE, while 43% failed to report tests of LD, and 18% of all studies did not report either test. About 14% of studies failed to report any sort of correction for multiple comparisons. Among stud- ies that reported corrections for HWE and LD, there was significant inconsistency in correction methods used. In studies that were inconsistent in their use of correction methods for tests of HWE, LD and differentiation, Hauser et al. report evidence of preferring less‐ conservative corrections (e.g., B‐Y or B‐H based FDR methods) to selectively “discover” loci that are significantly differentiated among populations. They also report significant use of more conservative corrections for tests of HWE and LD. Their findings are a jarring reminder of the importance of rigorous peer‐review and perhaps the unconscious biases on part of population geneticists to (i) not throw out their data for lack of concordance with HWE, or (ii) linkage equi- librium, and (iii) selectively maintain genomic loci that are signifi- We replicated this study with 205 papers mined using Google Scholar from the recent literature (2013–2018) (see Supplementary File 1 for a full list of surveyed literature), searching for “population genetics” studies, separated by phylum/kingdom/class (Mammalia, Arthropoda, Plants, Aves, Fish, Reptilia, Amphibia). Only studies that utilized short tandem repeat (STR—e.g., microsatellite) markers, or single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNP's) were retained. Studies were further filtered based on the tests that were performed as part of their methods—specifically, we searched for tests of “HWE,” “Link- age Equilibrium/Disequilibrium” and “differentiation.” All 205 studies were then scored using the rubric of Hauser et al., noting if the studies had performed a correction for multiple comparisons while performing tests of HWE, LD and differentiation.

Of these, 15% studies utilized SNP data, while a large majority (87%) studies utilized STR markers, with some studies using both. About 87% of all 205 studies report tests of HWE, whereas only 46% of those studies report any correction for tests of HWE (Table 1, Fig- ure 2c). About 75% report tests of LD (Figure 1), out of which only 48% report performing any correction for multiple testing of LD (Table 1, Figure 2d). The number of studies that report any test of differentiation was comparable to Hauser et al., with 179 studies (Figure 1). The same test between tests of LD and differentiation also rejected the null hypothesis of independence (p‐value < .0001). This indicates inconsistent use of correction methods within studies that per- formed tests of HWE and differentiation, or tests of LD and differ- entiation, among studies that report corrections for these tests. A chi‐squared goodness of fit test was used to test the null hypothesis that less‐conservative corrections (FDR) were used more often for tests of differentiation than expected by chance than in tests of HWE were much alike the findings of Hauser et al., 2018 (Χ2 = 50.12, p‐value < .0001). The same test for studies that cor- rected for multiple comparisons in tests of LD, and tests of differen- tiation also indicated a directional bias (Χ2 = 40.85, p‐value = 5.2e‐6), in that studies that used inconsistent correction methods were lar- gely using less‐conservative corrections for tests of differentiation, TABLE 1 Summary of studies that report tests of Hardy– Weinberg Equilibrium (HWE) and Linkage Disequilibrium (LD) in our survey of 205 population genetics studies FIGU RE 1 Summaries of studies in Hauser et al. 2018, vs. this study, describing the total number of studies that performed tests of HWE, LD and differentiation Our results, in conjunction with Hauser et al., 2018, clearly indi- cate a pattern of continued disuse and, when used, misuse of FWER/FDR correction methods for multiple comparisons in popula- tion genetics studies, despite numerous calls to disavow spurious p‐ value abuse, and inflated false discovery rates. We want to echo the sentiment of Hauser et al. (2018), in that there is currently no con- sensus on the most appropriate correction (Moran, 2003, but see Narum (2006) and White et al. (2018) for some guidelines on num- ber of statistical tests and false discovery rates). Authors should be aware of different tolerance levels for type 1 errors (false positives) and type II errors (false negatives), and in some cases, inconsistencies in applied correction methods across tests of HWE, LD and differentiation may be imperative.
